Variables.exp: Variables are containers for storing data values.

Data Types.exp: JavaScript has dynamic types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, object, symbol, bigint.
Data Types.code: let name = "Alice"; let age = 30; let isStudent = true;

Operators.exp: Operators perform operations on variables and values.

Control Flow.exp: Control flow statements control the execution order of code.

Loops.exp: Loops repeat code execution based on conditions.

Comments.exp: Comments explain code and are ignored during execution.
Comments.code:
// This is a single-line comment
/* This is a multi-line comment */

Strict Mode: Use 'use strict' to enable a safer, more predictable subset of JavaScript behavior and avoid common silent errors.

'use strict';                      // enables strict mode — catches silent errors
function check() {                 // strict mode applies in function scope
  x = 5; // ReferenceError in strict mode
}

Strict Mode.prompt: What happens when you assign to an undeclared variable in strict mode?
Strict Mode.explanation: In strict mode, assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of creating a global variable. This prevents accidental globals.

Strict Mode.prompt: Fix this code so it declares the variable properly instead of creating an accidental global:
Strict Mode.hint: Add a declaration keyword (let or const) before the variable.

What is JavaScript: JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted language that runs in browsers and on servers (Node.js). It has good parts (functions as first-class citizens, objects, closures) and bad parts (global variables, type coercion quirks). Crockford's 'The Good Parts' advises avoiding the bad parts by using strict mode, === over ==, and minimizing global scope. A key insight from Eloquent JavaScript: think of JavaScript as a language where functions are values that can be passed around, making it deeply rooted in functional programming patterns alongside its imperative style.

console.log('Hello JavaScript');  // prints string to browser console

// The good parts: functions are values
const greet = function(name) { return 'Hello ' + name; };  // assign anonymous function to variable
console.log(greet('World'));  // invoke function, logs result

options: Prints output to the browser console
What is JavaScript.explanation: console.log() prints its arguments to the browser's developer console. It's the most common way to debug JavaScript.

What is JavaScript.prompt: Complete the function that greets a user by name:

Syntax & Comments: JavaScript syntax is C-like with semicolons, blocks, and case-sensitivity. Crockford recommends always using semicolons — automatic semicolon insertion (ASI) can break code when lines start with ( or [. Comments should explain WHY, not WHAT. Eloquent JavaScript emphasizes clean formatting: consistent indentation (2 spaces), meaningful names, and breaking complex expressions into smaller named pieces.
Statements & Blocks: Learn how statement groups and block scope work with braces, and why grouping code carefully helps avoid bugs.

if (true) {           // always true, block executes
  let count = 1;       // declare block-scoped variable
  console.log(count);  // logs 1, count is block-scoped
}
JavaScript Engines: JavaScript engines: V8 (Chrome, Node.js, Deno), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari), Chakra (Edge legacy). All implement ECMAScript spec. Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation: Ignition (interpreter) + TurboFan (optimizing compiler) in V8. Engines add hooks via the host environment (browser APIs, Node.js APIs). The ECMAScript spec defines the language; engines may extend it.

Math Object.exp: The Math object provides mathematical constants and functions.

Type Conversion.exp: JavaScript can convert between types implicitly or explicitly.

Array Methods: Eloquent JavaScript calls array methods like map, filter, and reduce 'higher-order functions' — functions that operate on other functions. They enable a declarative style: you describe WHAT you want, not HOW. This is more readable and less error-prone than manual for loops. map transforms each element, filter selects elements, reduce combines elements into a single value, find locates the first match, some checks if any element matches, every checks if all match. The Good Parts cautions against mutating arrays while iterating — use map/filter to create new arrays instead.

Array Iteration.exp: Arrays can be iterated with forEach, map, filter, reduce.

Sets.exp: Sets store unique values of any type.

Maps.exp: Maps store key-value pairs with any type keys.

Destructuring: Unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables. Supports nested destructuring, default values, and rest patterns. Common mistake: trying to destructure null or undefined — throws TypeError. Best practice: provide defaults for safe destructuring; use renaming (object: { oldName: newName }) to avoid naming conflicts.

Spread Operator.exp: The spread operator expands iterables into elements.

JSON Methods.exp: JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() convert between JSON and objects.

Arrays: Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Arrays are objects — typeof [] returns 'object'. The length property is auto-updated but can be set manually (truncates or creates empty slots). Common mistake: using for...in on arrays (iterates keys as strings and includes inherited properties). Best practice: use array literal [] over new Array(); use for...of, forEach, or array methods (map/filter) for iteration.

const fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];
console.log(fruits[0]);        // 'apple' — zero-indexed
console.log(fruits.length);    // 3

const arr = new Array(3);      // [empty × 3] — creates sparse array!
console.log(arr.length);       // 3
console.log(arr[0]);           // undefined (empty slot)

// Methods that mutate
fruits.push('date');           // add to end
fruits.pop();                  // remove from end
fruits.unshift('apricot');     // add to start
fruits.shift();                // remove from start

// Checking arrays
console.log(Array.isArray(fruits)); // true — use this, not typeof
Map & Set: Map stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type (objects, functions, primitives) — unlike objects which only accept strings/symbols. Map preserves insertion order and has O(1) lookup. Set stores unique values of any type. Common mistake: using objects as maps — object keys are always strings; Map keys preserve type (number key 1 !== string key '1'). Best practice: use Map over plain objects for dynamic key collections; use Set for deduplication and fast membership checks.
WeakMap & WeakSet: WeakMap holds 'weak' references to object keys — if no other reference to the key exists, the entry is garbage collected. WeakSet similarly holds weak references to objects. Not iterable and no .size property because the contents could change anytime due to GC. Common mistake: expecting WeakMap/WeakSet to be iterable or have .size — they don't by design. Best practice: use WeakMap for private data (closure alternative), caching associated with DOM elements, or preventing memory leaks from long-lived references.
Iterators & Generators: Iterators are objects with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Any object with [Symbol.iterator] is iterable (works with for...of, spread, destructuring). Generators (function*) simplify iterator creation — they pause at each yield and resume on the next call. Common mistake: generators are single-use iterables — you can't restart them; create a new generator each time. Best practice: use generators for lazy sequences, infinite streams, and async iteration (async function*).

Prototypes.code:
function Person(name) { this.name = name; }
Person.prototype.greet = function() { return "Hi " + this.name; };

Classes.exp: ES6 classes provide a cleaner syntax for OOP.
Classes.code: class Animal { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } speak() {} }

Getters & Setters.code: class Person { get fullName() { return this.first + " " + this.last; } }

this Keyword.exp: The "this" keyword refers to the current execution context.
this Keyword.code: const obj = { name: "test", log: function() { console.log(this.name); } };

Bind Call Apply.exp: These methods explicitly set the value of "this".

Static Methods.exp: Static methods belong to the class itself, not instances.
Static Methods.code:
class MathUtils { static add(a,b) { return a+b; } }
MathUtils.add(2,3);

Private Fields.exp: Private fields are accessible only within the class.

Arrow Functions.exp: Arrow functions provide a concise function syntax.

Closures.exp: A closure is a function with access to its outer scope.
Closures.code: function outer(x) { return function(y) { return x + y; }; }

Higher-Order Functions.exp: Functions that take or return other functions.

Recursion.exp: A function that calls itself to solve problems.
Recursion.code: function factorial(n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); }

Rest Parameters.exp: Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array.

Callbacks.exp: Functions passed as arguments to other functions.

Promises.exp: Promises represent eventual completion of async operations.

Async Await.code: async function getData() { const res = await fetch("/api"); return res.json(); }

Error Handling.exp: Try/catch blocks handle errors in async code.

Event Loop.exp: The event loop handles async operations in JS.

Fetch API.code: const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(data), headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"} });

Web Workers.exp: Web Workers run scripts in background threads.

Service Workers.exp: Service Workers act as network proxies for offline support.

DOM Manipulation: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's API for HTML. Select elements with querySelector (single) or querySelectorAll (NodeList). Modify content via textContent, innerHTML, or classList. Common mistake: using innerHTML when textContent is safer (innerHTML parses HTML and can introduce XSS). Best practice: cache DOM references in variables (querying the DOM is slow); use classList.add/remove/toggle instead of className string manipulation; prefer textContent over innerHTML for text-only changes.
Events: Events signal user interaction (click, keydown, submit, scroll). addEventListener(type, handler) attaches a handler. Events flow through three phases: capture (outer to inner), target, and bubble (inner to outer). Common mistake: using inline event handlers (onclick=) — they create global functions and only allow one handler per event. Best practice: use addEventListener over onclick; use event delegation (listen on parent) for dynamic child elements; call removeEventListener to prevent memory leaks.

Event Bubbling.exp: Events propagate from child to parent elements.

Event Delegation.exp: Handling events on multiple children via a parent.

Forms & Validation: Handle form submission, read input values, and validate before sending. The submit event fires on the form element (not the button). Access fields via the elements collection or by id. Use e.preventDefault() to stop submission and validate first. Common mistake: listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form — the form can also be submitted via Enter key. Best practice: validate on submit (not on every keystroke for performance); use the Constraint Validation API (required, minlength, pattern attributes) for basic checks.
Fetch API: fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object. The Response must be parsed (.json(), .text()) before data is available. fetch only rejects on network errors — HTTP errors (404, 500) still resolve. Common mistake: forgetting that fetch doesn't reject on HTTP error status — check response.ok. Best practice: always handle network errors with .catch(); use AbortController to cancel in-flight requests; set appropriate Content-Type headers for POST/PUT.
Local Storage: localStorage persists data across browser sessions (no expiration). sessionStorage persists only for the current tab session — cleared when the tab closes. Both store strings only — objects must be serialized with JSON.stringify/parse. Storage limit is ~5-10MB per origin. Common mistake: storing objects directly — they become '[object Object]'; always use JSON.stringify. Best practice: wrap localStorage access in try/catch (private browsing may throw); use JSON for structured data; clear unused keys to stay under quota.
Timers: setTimeout runs a function once after a delay; setInterval runs repeatedly at the interval. Both return an ID passed to clearTimeout/clearInterval to cancel. Common mistake: assuming setInterval runs at exact intervals — if the callback takes longer than the interval, calls stack up. Best practice: use recursive setTimeout instead of setInterval for precise timing; always clear timers in cleanup code to prevent memory leaks; use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations (more efficient than setTimeout).
Web APIs (File, Drag, Clipboard): Modern Web APIs: File API (read files via FileReader), Drag & Drop (dragstart/dragover/drop events), Clipboard API (navigator.clipboard read/write), Geolocation, Web Storage, Web Workers. FileReader.readAsText/DataURL for preview. Clipboard.writeText/readText for copy/paste. Check API support with feature detection before use.

Try Catch.code: try { riskyCode(); } catch (err) { console.error(err.message); } finally { cleanup(); }

Custom Errors.code: class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(msg) { super(msg); this.name = "ValidationError"; } }

Source Maps.exp: Maps compiled code back to source code.

ES Modules.code: import { func } from "./module.js"; export const value = 42;

Bundlers.exp: Tools that bundle JS files for production.

Transpilers.exp: Tools that convert modern JS to older syntax.
Transpilers.code: Babel converts ES6+ to ES5 for browser compatibility.

Linters.exp: Tools that analyze code for potential errors.
Linters.code: ESLint: static analysis tool for JS/TS

WeakRef.exp: Weak references for garbage collection sensitive caching.
WeakRef.code: const ref = new WeakRef(obj); const val = ref.deref();

Memory Management.code: Allocation, usage, and garbage collection phases.

Garbage Collection.code: Mark-and-sweep algorithm; generational GC in V8.

Memory Leaks.code: Global variables, forgotten timers, detached DOM nodes, closures.

Debouncing.exp: Delaying function execution until after a pause.
Debouncing.code: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timer; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay); }; }

Throttling.code: function throttle(fn, limit) { let inThrottle; return (...args) => { if (!inThrottle) { fn(...args); inThrottle = true; setTimeout(() => inThrottle = false, limit); } }; }

Caching Strategies.code: Memoization, request caching, service worker cache.

Code Splitting.exp: Splitting code into chunks loaded on demand.
Code Splitting.code: Dynamic import() enables code splitting in bundlers.

Tree Shaking.code: Using ES modules enables tree shaking in bundlers like Webpack.

Lazy Loading.code: IntersectionObserver for lazy loading images and components.

var let const: The Good Parts advises never using var — it leaks scope and causes subtle bugs. Use const by default, let only when reassignment is needed. const doesn't mean immutable, only that the binding can't change.
Primitive Types: JavaScript has 7 primitive types. Primitives are immutable (you can't change them — operations return new values). typeof null returns 'object' (a JS bug from day one).

typeof 'text';      // 'string' — textual data
typeof 42;          // 'number' — 64-bit float (int & decimal)
typeof 1n;          // 'bigint' — arbitrary precision integer
typeof true;        // 'boolean' — true or false
typeof undefined;   // 'undefined' — declared but not assigned
typeof Symbol();    // 'symbol' — unique identifier
typeof null;        // 'object' — ⚠️ known JS bug (null is primitive)

// Number quirk: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);  // 0.30000000000000004 (IEEE 754 float)
Reference Types: Objects, arrays, and functions are reference types: variables hold a pointer to the value in memory. Assigning or passing copies the reference, not the value — mutating one affects the other. Use spread or structuredClone() for copies.

const obj = { name: 'Doge' };     // create object literal
const copy = obj;                    // copy is a REFERENCE (not a new object)
copy.name = 'Buddy';                 // mutates original via reference
console.log(obj.name);               // 'Buddy' — original changed too!

// Shallow copy with spread
const shallow = { ...obj };          // spreads own properties into new object

// Deep copy (handles nested)
const original = { a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } };  // nested object
const deep = structuredClone(original);        // deep copy, no shared refs
deep.nested.b = 99;                            // modify deep copy only
console.log(original.nested.b);                // 2 — independent
Truthy & Falsy: Every value coerces to boolean in conditionals. Crockford calls JavaScript's falsy rules 'a land of false promises' — learn them exactly to avoid bugs. Only 7 falsy values exist: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. The tricky one: empty arrays [] and objects {} are truthy. Eloquent JavaScript shows a practical pattern: use explicit Boolean() or !! for clarity, and avoid relying on coercion in complex conditions.
Type Conversion: JavaScript is weakly typed — it converts types automatically. This is convenient but dangerous. The Good Parts: always use === and explicit conversion.

'5' + 1;            // '51' — + triggers string concat when one is string
'5' - 1;            // 4 — - forces number conversion
Number('10');       // 10 — explicit string → number
String(42);         // '42' — explicit number → string
Boolean(1);         // true — explicit conversion

// Loose equality pitfalls (avoid these)
5 == '5';           // true — ⚠️ coercion hides bug
'' == false;        // true — ⚠️
null == undefined;  // true — ⚠️ special rule

// Use strict equality instead
5 === '5';          // false — ✅ correct
Template Literals: Template literals use backticks (`) instead of quotes. Embed expressions with ${}. They support multi-line without \n.
null vs undefined: undefined means a variable was declared but not assigned. null is intentionally empty — you assign it explicitly. They are different types.
Symbol & BigInt: Symbol creates unique, immutable identifiers for object properties. BigInt represents integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER using n suffix.

const sym = Symbol('id');      // create unique symbol key
const obj = { [sym]: 'secret' }; // use symbol as property key
console.log(obj[sym]);           // access property via symbol

const big = 9007199254740991n;   // bigint literal with n suffix
console.log(big + 1n);           // arithmetic works with bigints

Arithmetic Operators: Standard math: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), % (remainder/modulo), ** (exponentiation). Prefix/postfix ++ and -- increment/decrement by 1. Common mistake: + also does string concatenation — if either operand is a string, both are coerced to strings. Best practice: use parentheses to clarify operator precedence; avoid relying on ++ inside expressions.

console.log(10 + 3);   // 13
console.log(10 - 3);   // 7
console.log(10 * 3);   // 30
console.log(10 / 3);   // 3.333... (float, not floor)
console.log(10 % 3);   // 1 (remainder)
console.log(2 ** 4);   // 16 (exponentiation)

// + with strings triggers concatenation
console.log(1 + '2');  // '12' (string, not 3)
console.log(1 + 2 + '3'); // '33' (left to right: 1+2=3, then 3+'3')
Comparison Operators: Compare values and return a boolean. Relational: >, <, >=, <=. Equality: === (strict, no coercion) and == (loose, coerces types). Common mistake: using == allows type coercion (e.g., 5 == '5' is true), which causes subtle bugs. Best practice: always use === and !==; use Object.is() for NaN comparisons (Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true, unlike NaN === NaN which is false).
Logical Operators: && (AND) returns the first falsy operand or the last truthy one. || (OR) returns the first truthy operand or the last falsy one. ! (NOT) inverts truthiness and always returns boolean. Common mistake: && and || short-circuit — if the left operand determines the result, the right operand is never evaluated. This means side effects in the right operand may not run. Best practice: use || for default values and && for conditional execution, but beware that 0, '', and false are falsy so defaults may not work as expected — use ?? for null/undefined only.
Assignment Operators: Compound assignment combines an operation with assignment: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, **=, &&=, ||=, ??= (ES2021). They update the variable in place. Common mistake: ??= only assigns if the current value is null or undefined — unlike ||= which assigns for any falsy value. Best practice: prefer compound assignment for clarity when updating a variable relative to its current value.
Ternary Operator: The conditional (ternary) operator takes three operands: condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse. It's an expression, not a statement — it returns a value that can be assigned or used inline. Common mistake: nesting ternaries makes code unreadable — use if/else for more than one condition. Best practice: use ternaries for simple yes/no branches; keep them on one line for readability.
Spread & Rest: Spread (...) expands iterables (arrays, strings, objects) into individual elements. Rest (...) collects remaining elements into an array or object. Common mistake: spread creates a shallow copy — nested objects are still referenced, not cloned. Best practice: use spread for immutable updates (copying arrays/objects) and rest for flexible function parameters and destructuring.

If Else: Branch execution based on boolean conditions. The condition is coerced to boolean — any truthy value passes. Common mistake: assigning (=) instead of comparing (==) in conditions — 'if (x = 5)' assigns 5 (truthy) and always runs. Best practice: use curly braces even for single statements; prefer === over == for comparisons; use early returns (guard clauses) to reduce nesting.
Else If: else if chains additional conditions after if. Each condition is evaluated in order — the first true match runs and the rest are skipped. Use else if when exactly one branch should execute.
Switch Statement: Multi-way branching comparing the same expression to multiple values using strict equality (===). Use break to prevent fall-through to the next case. Common mistake: forgetting break causes execution to fall through to the next case (sometimes intentional). Best practice: always include break (or return); use default for unmatched values; consider if/else for ranges (switch is for discrete values only).
for Loops: Three types: for (init; condition; increment) — classic counted loop. for...of iterates over values of iterables (arrays, strings, Map, Set). for...in iterates over enumerable property keys of objects. Common mistake: using for...in for arrays (iterates keys as strings, includes inherited properties). Best practice: use for...of for arrays, for...in for objects, and classic for when you need the index.
while & do while: while checks the condition before each iteration — may run zero times. do...while checks after — always runs at least once. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable causes infinite loops (hangs the browser). Best practice: prefer for loops when you know the iteration count; use while for condition-controlled loops (reading input, waiting for a state change).
break & continue: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next. With labeled statements, break and continue can control outer loops from inside nested ones. Common mistake: using break in forEach() callback — it doesn't work (forEach doesn't respect break). Best practice: use labeled breaks sparingly (they can make control flow hard to follow); prefer extracting to a function with early return.
Nested Loops: A loop inside another loop. Each outer iteration triggers a full inner loop run. Complexity is O(n*m) — a 100×100 grid runs 10,000 iterations. Use labeled break/continue to control outer loops from inside. Common mistake: quadratic complexity on large datasets can freeze the browser. Best practice: consider flatMap(), combined data structures, or early termination when possible.
Error Handling: try/catch/finally handles runtime exceptions. try runs the risky code; catch receives the error object; finally always runs (even after return). Common mistake: catching and ignoring errors silently — always log or re-throw. Best practice: catch specific error types when possible; use finally for cleanup (closing files, clearing state); throw custom Error objects (not strings or numbers) for stack traces.

Function Declarations: Functions are the fundamental building block of JavaScript. Eloquent JavaScript calls them 'values that contain behavior'. Function declarations are hoisted (moved to top), which Crockford considers useful for organizing code top-down. A function always returns something — undefined if no explicit return. The Good Parts says: 'functions are the best part of JavaScript' — they create scope, enable modularity, and are the only way to create private variables. Every function has access to the scope in which it was defined (closure), making them powerful tools for encapsulation.
Function Expressions: A function expression assigns a function to a variable. Unlike declarations, function expressions are NOT hoisted — you can't call them before the definition line. Named function expressions have a name property for debugging but the name is only visible inside the function scope. Common mistake: expecting function expressions to be hoisted like declarations. Best practice: use const for function expressions to prevent reassignment; use named expressions for better stack traces in recursion and debugging.
Arrow Functions: Arrow functions provide shorter syntax: (params) => expression. Key differences from regular functions: they inherit this from the enclosing scope (lexical this), cannot be used as constructors (no new), and don't have arguments object. Common mistake: using arrow functions for object methods — this won't refer to the object. Best practice: use arrow functions for callbacks, array methods (map/filter/reduce), and when you want lexical this; use regular functions for object methods, constructors, and when you need dynamic this.
Default Parameters: Default parameter values are used when the argument is undefined (not when it's null or other falsy values). Defaults can be expressions or even function calls — they're evaluated at call time, not definition time. Common mistake: thinking defaults trigger on null — they only trigger on undefined. Best practice: put default parameters after required ones so calling code can skip them; avoid complex default expressions that hide bugs.
Rest Parameters: Rest parameters (...) collect remaining arguments into a real array (unlike the array-like arguments object). Must be the last parameter. Common mistake: confusing rest with the arguments object — arguments is array-like (no .map/.filter) and includes ALL parameters, not just the extras. Best practice: prefer rest over arguments for clarity; use rest in destructuring to capture remaining items.
Closures: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned. This is JavaScript’s most powerful pattern — it enables data privacy (module pattern), function factories, event handlers with state, and memoization. Common mistake: closures capture variables by reference, not by value — loop closures all see the final value unless you use let or an IIFE. Best practice: use closures for encapsulation (hide implementation details); be mindful of memory if the closure retains large objects.

Objects: Objects are the foundation of JavaScript — almost everything is an object or can behave like one. Crockford calls objects 'containers of properties, where each property has a name and a value'. Objects are passed by reference, making them efficient but also dangerous when mutated in place. Eloquent JavaScript describes objects as 'octopuses with any number of tentacles' — they can hold any type. The Good Parts recommends object literals as the simplest and safest way to create objects, avoiding new Object() and similar verbose forms.
This Keyword: this is one of JavaScript's most misunderstood features. Crockford calls this 'a source of enormous confusion'. Its value depends entirely on HOW a function is called: method call → the object, plain call → undefined (strict) or global (sloppy), constructor call (new) → the new instance, call/apply/bind → explicitly set. Eloquent JavaScript calls this 'the function's context'. Arrow functions avoid the confusion by inheriting this from the enclosing scope — Crockford recommends using them for callbacks. The Good Parts says: 'this is always bound to the global object in inner functions' — capture it with a variable (that = this) or use arrow functions.
Prototypes: Prototypal inheritance is JavaScript's native inheritance model. Crockford explains: 'a prototype is an object from which other objects inherit properties'. Unlike classical inheritance (classes inherit from classes), objects inherit directly from objects. Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. The Good Parts advocates for prototypal over classical inheritance — it's simpler and more flexible. Eloquent JavaScript describes the prototype chain as 'a series of objects linked together' ending at Object.prototype. When you access a property, JavaScript walks the chain until found. Favor composition over inheritance in large systems.
Classes: Class syntax (ES2015) is sugar over prototypes: class defines a constructor, methods go on the prototype, and static methods go on the constructor itself. Supports extends for inheritance and super for parent calls. Common mistake: thinking classes are a new inheritance model — they're still prototypal underneath. Best practice: use class syntax over manual prototype manipulation for readability; prefer composition over deep inheritance chains.
Inheritance: extends creates a subclass that inherits from a parent class. super() calls the parent constructor; super.method() calls a parent method. Subclasses can override methods and access parent implementations. Common mistake: forgetting to call super() in the subclass constructor — causes ReferenceError. Best practice: keep inheritance shallow (1-2 levels max); prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for code reuse.
Getters & Setters: Getters (get) and setters (set) let you define properties that call functions when accessed or assigned. They look like normal property access but can run validation, computation, or logging. Common mistake: getters should not have side effects (callers expect property-like behavior). Best practice: use getters for computed properties and setters for validation; avoid expensive operations in getters since callers don't expect function-call overhead.

Promises: A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never. States: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved), or rejected (error). .then() handles fulfillment, .catch() handles rejection, .finally() runs regardless. Promises are microtasks — they resolve before macrotasks like setTimeout. Common mistake: not returning the promise from .then() breaks the chain — the next .then() receives undefined. Best practice: always return promises from chains; handle rejection at the end of the chain (not per-link); use Promise.all for parallel work.
Async/Await: async functions always return a Promise. await pauses execution until the awaited promise settles — but only within the async function (the caller continues). Common mistake: calling async functions without awaiting them — they still run but you lose the return value and error handling. Best practice: wrap await calls in try/catch for error handling; use Promise.all for independent parallel async operations (sequential await is slower); top-level await works in ES modules.
Fetch & HTTP: fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise<Response>. Always check response.ok — fetch only rejects on network errors, not HTTP errors. GET is default; POST/PUT/PATCH require method and body. Common mistake: not checking response.ok — a 404 resolves successfully. Best practice: always check .ok and throw for non-2xx; use AbortController for timeout/cancellation; set Content-Type for requests with body.
Event Loop: The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model — single-threaded but non-blocking. Eloquent JavaScript explains: 'when a program needs to wait, it schedules a callback and continues running other code'. The call stack runs synchronously; async callbacks go to the task queue. Promises and async/await use the microtask queue (higher priority than macrotasks like setTimeout). This means promise callbacks run BEFORE timer callbacks, even zero-delay timers. Crockford says: 'understanding the event loop is essential — everything in JavaScript happens in a single thread, and if you block it, the whole page freezes'.
Web Workers: Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread — they can't access the DOM, window, or parent scope. Communicate with the main thread via postMessage() and onmessage. Workers are great for CPU-intensive tasks (image processing, data parsing, encryption). Common mistake: trying to access DOM or window inside a worker — not available. Best practice: use workers for expensive computations that would block the UI; use structuredClone or Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) for efficient data passing; terminate workers when done to free resources.
Async Iteration: Async iteration (for await...of) consumes async iterables with [Symbol.asyncIterator] that returns promises from next(). async function* defines an async generator. Useful for streaming data (paginated APIs, WebSocket messages, file chunks). Common mistake: using for...of instead of for await...of on async iterables — for...of doesn't await promises. Best practice: use async generators for streaming scenarios; handle errors inside the loop with try/catch.

ES Modules: Share code with import/export syntax, and run modules in modern browsers or bundlers.

export function hello() { return 'hi'; }  // named export
import { hello } from './module.js';        // named import from module
Spread Syntax: Expand iterable values into arrays or function calls, and merge object properties effortlessly.

const copy = [...[1, 2]];         // spread: expand iterable into array
const merged = { ...{ a: 1 }, b: 2 }; // spread: merge object properties
Optional Chaining: Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits to undefined if the value before ?. is null or undefined — without throwing. Works with property access (?.), method calls (?.()), and dynamic access (?.[]). Common mistake: thinking ?. prevents 'undefined is not a function' for methods that don't exist — it does, but only when the object itself is null/undefined. Best practice: combine ?. with ?? for safe deep access chains; don't overuse — if a value should always exist, let it throw (fail fast).
Nullish Coalescing: ?? returns the right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined. Unlike || which returns the right operand for ANY falsy value (0, '', false). Common mistake: using || for defaults when 0 or '' are valid values — || treats them as absent. Best practice: use ?? for default values when the left side could be a valid falsy value (empty string, zero, false); use || for truly absent values (when undefined/null and falsy should both get the default).
Dynamic Import: import() is a function-like expression that dynamically loads a module at runtime. It returns a Promise resolving to the module namespace object. Enables code splitting (load only what's needed), lazy loading (load on user interaction), and conditional imports (platform detection). Common mistake: dynamic imports are NOT hoisted — they execute when reached. Best practice: use dynamic imports for large libraries not needed on initial load (charts, editors, heavy utilities); combine with top-level await in module scripts.
Promise Combinators: Promise.all waits for ALL promises — rejects fast if ANY rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for ALL to settle (resolve or reject) — never rejects, returns results with status. Promise.race returns the first settled promise. Promise.any returns the first fulfilled promise — rejects only if ALL reject. Common mistake: using Promise.all when one failure shouldn't fail the whole batch — use allSettled. Best practice: use all for dependent parallel work (must all succeed), allSettled for independent results, race for timeouts, any for fastest success.
Records & Tuples (Proposal): Records and Tuples (Stage 2 proposal) add immutable compound primitives. Records (#{}) are like frozen objects; Tuples (#[]) are like frozen arrays. Compared by value, not reference. Use === naturally. Nested objects must be Records/Tuples. Polyfill available via @bloomberg/record-tuple. Browsers: enable via experimental flags.

React: React is a component-based UI library. Components return JSX (JavaScript XML) describing what to render. Props pass data from parent to child; state manages component-local data that triggers re-renders. Common mistake: mutating state directly (this.state.x = 5) instead of using setState or the state setter. Best practice: prefer functional components with hooks (useState, useEffect) over class components; keep components small and focused; lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.
Vue: Vue is a progressive framework with reactive templates and a component system. Options API uses data(), methods, computed, and watch. Composition API (setup) provides better code organization. Common mistake: using normal variables in data() instead of reactive ref() or reactive() — Vue can only track reactive objects. Best practice: prefer the Composition API for complex logic reuse; use computed for derived state instead of methods in templates; use v-bind:key in v-for for efficient re-rendering.
Express: Express is a minimalist Node.js web framework. Define routes with app.get/post/put/delete. Middleware functions (app.use) process requests in order — they can modify req/res, end the request, or call next(). Common mistake: forgetting to call next() in middleware — the request hangs. Best practice: structure routes with express.Router() for modularity; use error-handling middleware (4 args) for centralized errors; parse bodies with express.json() middleware.
Next.js: Next.js is a React framework for production with file-based routing (pages/ or app/), SSR/SSG, and API routes. Pages/ directory: each file becomes a route. App Router (app/) uses layouts, loading states, and server components. Common mistake: fetching data in client components when server components would be more efficient. Best practice: use server components for initial data fetching (rendered on server, smaller JS bundle); use getStaticProps (Pages Router) for SSG; leverage Suspense boundaries for streaming.
NestJS: NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework built with TypeScript that uses decorators for controllers, providers, modules, and middleware. It supports Express or Fastify under the hood. Common mistake: forgetting to register providers in module decorators — unregistered providers cause runtime injection errors. Best practice: use modules to organize features; keep controllers thin (delegate logic to services); leverage dependency injection for testability.
Vite: Vite is a fast build tool that uses native ES modules for dev (instant HMR) and Rollup for production builds. Supports JS, TS, JSX, CSS, and assets out of the box. Common mistake: thinking Vite only works for frontend frameworks — it works with vanilla JS and library development too. Best practice: use vite.config.js for custom configuration (aliases, plugins, proxy); leverage HMR for fast iteration.

JSON: JSON.parse converts JSON strings to objects; JSON.stringify serializes objects to JSON strings. Essential for data exchange and API communication. Common mistake: JSON.parse throws on invalid JSON — always wrap in try/catch or use a safe parser. Best practice: use JSON.stringify's replacer and space arguments for controlled serialization; avoid storing undefined, BigInt, or circular references — they're silently dropped or throw.
Math & Number: Math provides constants and methods for math operations: random, floor, round, ceil, max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, sin, cos, PI, E. Number offers parseInt, parseFloat, isNaN, isFinite, isInteger, and EPSILON. Common mistake: using Math.floor for rounding — use Math.round for standard rounding and Math.trunc for integer truncation. Best practice: use Number.isNaN over global isNaN (global coerces, Number.isNaN doesn't); use Math.max/Math.min with spread for arrays; avoid floating-point equality checks — use epsilon comparison.

console.log(Math.PI);                 // 3.14159...
console.log(Math.random());             // random float 0–1
console.log(Math.floor(3.9));           // 3 (round down)
console.log(Math.round(3.5));           // 4 (standard rounding)
console.log(Math.trunc(-3.9));          // -3 (remove decimal, no rounding)
console.log(Math.max(1, 5, 3));        // 5
console.log(Math.max(...[1, 5, 3]));   // 5 (spread array)
console.log(Number.parseInt('42px'));   // 42 (parses until non-digit)
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN));         // true (no coercion)
console.log(Number.isFinite(Infinity)); // false
console.log(Number.isInteger(3.0));     // true
console.log(Number.EPSILON);            // ~2.2e-16 (for float comparison)
Date & Time: Date handles date/time operations: creation, formatting, arithmetic, and timezone handling. Months are zero-indexed (0 = January). Date objects are mutable — all set methods mutate in place. Common mistake: date parsing with strings is unreliable across browsers — use Date.parse cautiously or a date library. Best practice: use toISOString() for storage/serialization; use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localized display; use timestamps (Date.now()) for calculations to avoid month-index confusion.
String Methods: Strings have built-in methods for manipulation: slice, substring, split, replace/replaceAll, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, trim, includes, startsWith, endsWith, repeat, padStart/padEnd, match, matchAll, and charAt. Strings are immutable — all methods return a new string. Common mistake: confusing slice (accepts negative indices) with substring (treats negative as 0). Best practice: use replaceAll (ES2021) over replace with global regex for simpler replacement; use template literals for concatenation; use includes over indexOf for readability.
Proxy & Reflect: Proxy wraps an object to intercept operations (get, set, delete, etc.) via traps. Reflect provides methods that mirror the default proxy behavior for forwarding.
Intl API: Intl provides locale-aware formatting for dates, numbers, currencies, and collation. Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, and ListFormat are the most common.

const date = new Date();                           // current date
const df = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('de-DE', { dateStyle: 'full' }); // German locale
console.log(df.format(date));                      // localized date string

const nf = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
console.log(nf.format(1234.56));                   // '$1,234.56'
TypedArrays (ArrayBuffer): TypedArrays provide views over raw binary data in an ArrayBuffer. Types include Int8Array, Uint8Array, Float64Array, and more for performance-critical work.

const buf = new ArrayBuffer(16);   // allocate 16 bytes of memory
const view = new Float64Array(buf);   // 64-bit float view over buffer
view[0] = 3.14159;                    // write float at index 0
console.log(view[0]);                 // read back: 3.14159
// Also useful for WebSocket/WebRTC binary protocols
structuredClone & Deep Copy: structuredClone creates a deep copy of an object, handling circular references and types like Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and Blob.

const original = { name: 'Doge', tags: ['cool', 'fun'], meta: { created: new Date() } };
const clone = structuredClone(original);             // deep copy everything
clone.tags.push('smart');                             // modify clone only
console.log(original.tags);                           // ['cool', 'fun']
console.log(clone.tags);                              // ['cool', 'fun', 'smart']
Intl & Localization: Intl API provides locale-sensitive formatting: Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.Collator, Intl.ListFormat, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, Intl.PluralRules, Intl.Segmenter. The locale string ('en-US', 'de-DE', 'ja-JP') determines formatting rules. Use options for fine-grained control. Intl.DateTimeFormat handles timezone, calendar, numbering systems.

Hoisting Explained: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution. var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined — accessing them before declaration returns undefined, not ReferenceError. let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized — they exist in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block start until declaration, so accessing them throws ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted entirely (body included), so they can be called before their definition. Function expressions are NOT hoisted — use them only after the assignment line.
Global Scope: The global scope is the outermost scope. In browsers, window is the global object; in Node.js, it's global. Variables declared with var at the top level become properties of the global object. let, const, and class at the top level do NOT become global object properties — they exist in the global scope but are not properties of window/global. Relying on global variables is considered bad practice — they create naming conflicts and make code hard to reason about. The Good Parts: minimize global scope by using IIFEs or modules.
Lexical Scoping: Lexical (static) scoping means a variable's scope is determined by its position in the source code, not by how functions are called at runtime. Inner functions can access variables from outer scopes, but not vice versa. This is the foundation of closures — a function remembers the scope in which it was defined. JavaScript has no dynamic scoping — this is not scope, it's context (determined by call pattern). Understanding lexical scope helps predict which variables are accessible at any point in the code.
Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): TDZ is the region from block start to variable declaration where let/const/class variables exist but can't be accessed. ReferenceError: Cannot access before initialization. typeof also throws (unlike var/undeclared). TDZ prevents accessing variables before they're initialized. Class declarations are also hoisted but not initialized (TDZ applies).

Object.is: Object.is (ES6) compares two values for equality. It behaves like === except for two edge cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true (NaN === NaN is false), and Object.is(0, -0) returns false (0 === -0 is true). Use Object.is when you need NaN equivalence or need to distinguish signed zeros. For most cases, === is sufficient and more readable. Object.is does NOT perform deep object comparison — references must match. It's available on all modern platforms and polyfillable for older ones.
SameValueZero: SameValueZero is an equality algorithm used by Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes. It behaves like Object.is but treats -0 and 0 as equal. This means NaN is considered equal to itself (unlike ===) but -0 equals 0 (unlike Object.is). It's not directly callable in user code but is used internally by Set.has(), Map.has(), and includes(). Understanding it helps explain why Set.has(NaN) returns true but indexOf(NaN) returns -1.
Object.is & SameValue: Object.is() compares value equality (SameValue algorithm), similar to === but with two differences: +0 !== -0, and NaN === NaN. SameValueZero (used in Map, Set, includes) treats +0 and -0 as equal. SameValue (Object.is) distinguishes them. Use Object.is for NaN-safe comparisons. Most algorithms use SameValueZero for consistency.

The Event Loop: The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model: single-threaded, non-blocking, and asynchronous by necessity. The call stack runs synchronous code. When an async operation completes, its callback is queued. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) go to the task queue. Microtasks (Promise.then, async/await, queueMicrotask) go to the microtask queue. After each macrotask, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue before processing the next macrotask. This means promise callbacks run before setTimeout callbacks, even zero-delay ones. Blocking the call stack with long synchronous work freezes the page.
Microtasks vs Macrotasks: Microtasks include Promise.then/catch/finally, MutationObserver, and queueMicrotask. Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, and UI rendering (browser). After every macrotask, the event loop processes all pending microtasks before the next macrotask or render. This is why Promise-based code runs before timer callbacks. queueMicrotask() explicitly schedules a microtask. Microtasks can starve the event loop if they continuously enqueue more microtasks — causing the page to become unresponsive despite no single long task.
Callbacks: A callback is a function passed to another function for later execution. They are the foundation of async JavaScript — used in setTimeout, event handlers, fs.readFile, and fetch. Callback-based code suffers from 'callback hell' (pyramid of doom) when nested. Modern alternatives: Promises and async/await. The error-first callback pattern (Node.js convention) passes error as the first argument: callback(err, result). Always handle errors in callbacks — unhandled errors silently disappear.
Microtasks & Event Loop: The event loop processes macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events) and microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver). Microtasks run immediately after the current macrotask, before the next macrotask. Await is syntactic sugar for .then(). process.nextTick (Node.js) runs before microtasks. requestAnimationFrame runs before repaint.

ES Modules (ESM): ES Modules (ES6) use import and export statements. Each module has its own scope — no global leakage. Named exports export multiple values with specific names. Default export exports a single main value per module. Dynamic import() (ES2020) loads modules on demand (returns a Promise). ESM is static — imports are hoisted and resolved before execution, enabling tree-shaking. Modules are strict by default. Use type='module' on script tags in browsers, or 'type': 'module' in package.json for Node.js.
CommonJS (CJS): CommonJS is Node.js's original module system using require() and module.exports. require() loads modules synchronously — fine for servers but not browsers. module.exports can be any value. exports is a shorthand reference to module.exports — reassigning exports breaks the reference. Node.js supports both CJS (file.js or .cjs) and ESM (.mjs or type='module' package.json). Use require() for dynamic conditional imports. CJS modules are not tree-shakeable because exports are determined at runtime.
Dynamic Import & Code Splitting: Dynamic import() returns a promise for a module namespace. Enables code splitting (load on demand), reducing initial bundle size. import.meta provides module metadata. import.meta.url (file URL), import.meta.resolve (spec resolution). Dynamic imports are not statically analyzable — bundlers may need hints for splitting. Top-level await works in modules.

Memory Lifecycle: JavaScript manages memory automatically via garbage collection. The lifecycle: (1) Allocate — memory is reserved when you create values (objects, arrays, closures, DOM nodes); (2) Use — references point to the allocated memory as your code runs; (3) Release — when a value is no longer reachable, its memory becomes eligible for garbage collection. Reachability means the value can be accessed from a root (global object, current call stack, active closures). Values can become unreachable when all references go out of scope, are reassigned, or set to null.
Garbage Collection: Modern JavaScript engines use generational garbage collection. Young generation: new objects are allocated here — collected frequently (minor GC) since most objects die young. Old generation: objects that survive multiple GC cycles are promoted here — collected less often (major GC). The mark-and-sweep algorithm: starting from roots (global object, stack, DOM), the GC marks all reachable objects, then sweeps (frees) unmarked objects. Common memory leaks: detached DOM elements (referenced in JS but removed from DOM), forgotten timers holding references, global variable accumulation, and closures retaining large unnecessary data.
WeakRef & FinalizationRegistry: WeakRef holds a weak reference to an object (doesn't prevent GC). Use .deref() to access (may return undefined). FinalizationRegistry registers cleanup callbacks when objects are garbage collected. Use cases: caching, DOM node lifecycle, resource cleanup. Not meant for general use — GC timing is unpredictable. Avoid in performance-critical paths.

Console Debugging: Browser DevTools console is essential for debugging. console.log() prints values. console.error() and console.warn() print with severity icons and stack traces. console.table() renders arrays/objects as sortable tables. console.time()/timeEnd() measures execution. console.group()/groupEnd() nests logs. console.count() counts calls. console.trace() prints the call stack. Using debugger; statement pauses execution. For real debugging, use Sources panel breakpoints — they're more precise than console.log scatterguns.
Performance Debugging: Performance debugging identifies slow code. Use the Performance panel to record activity: look for long tasks (>50ms block main thread), forced reflow (reading layout properties after DOM mutations), and layout thrash (alternating reads/writes in loops). Lighthouse audits performance. Use performance.now() for precise timing. The Network panel shows request timing and waterfall. Avoid: forcing layout with offsetWidth/Height in loops, heavy synchronous work on the main thread, and excessive DOM manipulations without batching.
Debugging Memory Leaks: Memory leaks cause page slowdown and crashes. Use the Memory panel to take heap snapshots — compare 'before' and 'after' to see retained objects. Common patterns: detached DOM nodes (elements referenced in JS but removed from DOM), closures holding large data, global caches without cleanup, forgotten timers/intervals, and event listeners not removed. Look for 'Detached HTML elements' in heap snapshots. The Performance panel's memory timeline shows heap growth over time — steady growth indicates a leak.
